{{short description|Type of transfinite numbers}}
{{about|a type of ordinal in mathematics|the physical constant ''ε<sub>0</sub>''|Vacuum permittivity}}
{{Technical|date=January 2023}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''epsilon numbers''' are a collection of [[transfinite number]]s whose defining property is that they are [[fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]]s of an <!-- Do not link 'exponential map': This has little to do with the exp maps of differential geometry --> '''exponential map'''. Consequently, they are not reachable from 0 via a finite series of applications of the chosen exponential map and of "weaker" operations like addition and multiplication.  The original epsilon numbers were introduced by [[Georg Cantor]] in the context of [[ordinal arithmetic]]; they are the [[ordinal number]]s ''ε'' that satisfy the [[equation]]
<math display="block">
 \varepsilon = \omega^\varepsilon,
</math>
in which {{mvar|ω}} is the smallest infinite ordinal.

The least such ordinal is '''''ε''<sub>0</sub>''' (pronounced '''epsilon nought''' (chiefly British), '''epsilon naught''' (chiefly American), or '''epsilon zero'''), which can be viewed as the "limit" obtained by [[transfinite recursion]] from a sequence of smaller limit ordinals:
<math display="block">
 \varepsilon_0 = \omega^{\omega^{\omega^{\cdot^{\cdot^\cdot}}}} = \sup \left\{ \omega, \omega^{\omega}, \omega^{\omega^\omega}, \omega^{\omega^{\omega^\omega}}, \dots \right\},
</math>
where {{math|sup}} is the [[supremum]], which is equivalent to [[set union]] in the case of the von Neumann representation of ordinals.

Larger ordinal fixed points of the exponential map are indexed by ordinal subscripts, resulting in <math>\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2, \ldots,\varepsilon_\omega, \varepsilon_{\omega+1}, \ldots, \varepsilon_{\varepsilon_0}, \ldots, \varepsilon_{\varepsilon_1}, \ldots, \varepsilon_{\varepsilon_{\varepsilon_{\cdot_{\cdot_{\cdot}}}}}, \ldots \zeta_0 = \varphi_2(0)</math>.<ref>Stephen G. Simpson, ''Subsystems of Second-order Arithmetic'' (2009, p.&nbsp;387).</ref> The ordinal {{math|''ε''<sub>0</sub>}} is still [[countable]], as is any epsilon number whose index is countable. [[Uncountable]] ordinals also exist, along with uncountable epsilon numbers whose index is an uncountable ordinal.

The smallest epsilon number {{math|''ε''<sub>0</sub>}} appears in many [[mathematical induction|induction]] proofs, because for many purposes [[transfinite induction]] is only required up to {{math|''ε''<sub>0</sub>}} (as in [[Gentzen's consistency proof]] and the proof of [[Goodstein's theorem]]). Its use by [[Gentzen]] to prove the consistency of [[Peano arithmetic]], along with [[Gödel's second incompleteness theorem]], show that Peano arithmetic cannot prove the [[Well-founded relation|well-foundedness]] of this ordering (it is in fact the least ordinal with this property, and as such, in [[proof theory|proof-theoretic]] [[ordinal analysis]], is used as a measure of the strength of the theory of Peano arithmetic).

Many larger epsilon numbers can be defined using the [[Veblen function]].

A more general class of epsilon numbers has been identified by [[John Horton Conway]] and [[Donald Knuth]] in the [[surreal number]] system, consisting of all surreals that are fixed points of the base-{{mvar|ω}} exponential map {{math|''x'' → ''ω''<sup>''x''</sup>}}.

{{harvtxt|Hessenberg|1906}} defined gamma numbers (see [[additively indecomposable ordinal]]) to be numbers {{math|''γ'' > 0}} such that {{math|1=''α'' + ''γ'' = ''γ''}} whenever {{math|''α'' < ''γ''}}, and delta numbers (see [[Additively indecomposable ordinal#Multiplicatively indecomposable|multiplicatively indecomposable ordinal]]) to be numbers {{math|''δ'' > 1}} such that {{math|1=''αδ'' = ''δ''}} whenever {{math|0 < ''α'' < ''δ''}}, and epsilon numbers to be numbers {{math|''ε'' > 2}} such that {{math|1=''α''<sup>''ε''</sup> = ''ε''}} whenever {{math|1 < ''α'' < ''ε''}}. His gamma numbers are those of the form {{math|''ω''<sup>''β''</sup>}}, and his delta numbers are those of the form {{math|''ω''<sup>''ω''<sup>''β''</sup></sup>}}.

== Ordinal ε numbers ==
{{unsourced section|date=February 2023}}

The standard definition of [[ordinal exponentiation]] with base α is:
*<math>\alpha^0 = 1 \,,</math>
*<math>\alpha^\beta = \alpha^{\beta-1} \cdot \alpha \,,</math> when <math>\beta</math> has an immediate predecessor <math>\beta - 1</math>.
*<math>\alpha^\beta=\sup \lbrace\alpha^\delta \mid 0 < \delta < \beta\rbrace</math>, whenever <math>\beta</math> is a [[limit ordinal]].

From this definition, it follows that for any fixed ordinal {{math|''α'' > 1}}, the [[map (mathematics)|mapping]] <math>\beta \mapsto \alpha^\beta</math>  is a [[normal function]], so it has arbitrarily large [[fixed point (mathematics)|fixed points]] by the [[fixed-point lemma for normal functions]].  When <math>\alpha = \omega</math>, these fixed points are precisely the ordinal epsilon numbers.
*<math>\varepsilon_0 = \sup \left\lbrace 1, \omega, \omega^\omega, \omega^{\omega^\omega}, \omega^{\omega^{\omega^\omega}}, \ldots\right\rbrace \,,</math>
*<math>\varepsilon_\beta = \sup \left\lbrace {\varepsilon_{\beta-1}+1}, \omega^{\varepsilon_{\beta-1}+1}, \omega^{\omega^{\varepsilon_{\beta-1}+1}}, \omega^{\omega^{\omega^{\varepsilon_{\beta-1}+1}}}, \ldots\right\rbrace \,,</math> when <math>\beta</math> has an immediate predecessor <math>\beta - 1</math>.
*<math>\varepsilon_\beta=\sup \lbrace \varepsilon_\delta \mid \delta < \beta \rbrace</math>, whenever <math>\beta</math> is a limit ordinal.

Because
:<math>\omega^{\varepsilon_0 + 1} = \omega^{\varepsilon_0} \cdot \omega^1 = \varepsilon_0 \cdot \omega \,,</math>
:<math>\omega^{\omega^{\varepsilon_0 + 1}} = \omega^{(\varepsilon_0 \cdot \omega)} = {(\omega^{\varepsilon_0})}^\omega = \varepsilon_0^\omega \,,</math>
:<math>\omega^{\omega^{\omega^{\varepsilon_0 + 1}}} = \omega^{{\varepsilon_0}^\omega} = \omega^{{\varepsilon_0}^{1+\omega}} = \omega^{(\varepsilon_0\cdot{\varepsilon_0}^\omega)} = {(\omega^{\varepsilon_0})}^{{\varepsilon_0}^\omega} = {\varepsilon_0}^{{\varepsilon_0}^\omega} \,,</math>
a different sequence with the same supremum, <math>\varepsilon_1</math>, is obtained by starting from 0 and exponentiating with base {{math|''ε''<sub>0</sub>}} instead:
:<math>\varepsilon_1 = \sup\left\{1, \varepsilon_0, {\varepsilon_0}^{\varepsilon_0}, {\varepsilon_0}^{{\varepsilon_0}^{\varepsilon_0}}, \ldots\right\}.</math>

Generally, the epsilon number <math>\varepsilon_{\beta}</math> indexed by any ordinal that has an immediate predecessor <math>\beta-1</math> can be constructed similarly.
:<math>\varepsilon_{\beta} = \sup\left\{1, \varepsilon_{\beta-1}, \varepsilon_{\beta-1}^{\varepsilon_{\beta-1}}, \varepsilon_{\beta-1}^{\varepsilon_{\beta-1}^{\varepsilon_{\beta-1}}}, \dots\right\}.</math>
In particular, whether or not the index β is a limit ordinal, <math>\varepsilon_\beta</math> is a fixed point not only of base {{mvar|ω}} exponentiation but also of base δ exponentiation for all ordinals <math>1 < \delta < \varepsilon_\beta</math>.

Since the epsilon numbers are an unbounded subclass of the ordinal numbers, they are enumerated using the ordinal numbers themselves.  For any ordinal number <math>\beta</math>, <math>\varepsilon_\beta</math> is the least epsilon number (fixed point of the exponential map) not already in the set <math>\{ \varepsilon_\delta\mid \delta < \beta \}</math>. It might appear that this is the non-constructive equivalent of the constructive definition using iterated exponentiation; but the two definitions are equally non-constructive at steps indexed by limit ordinals, which represent transfinite recursion of a higher order than taking the supremum of an exponential series.

The following facts about epsilon numbers are straightforward to prove:
* Although it is quite a large number, <math>\varepsilon_0</math> is still [[countable]], being a countable union of countable ordinals; in fact, <math>\varepsilon_\beta</math> is countable if and only if <math>\beta</math> is countable.
* The union (or supremum) of any [[empty set|non-empty]] set of epsilon numbers is an epsilon number; so for instance <math display="block">\varepsilon_\omega = \sup\{\varepsilon_0, \varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2, \ldots\}</math> is an epsilon number.  Thus, the mapping <math>\beta \mapsto \varepsilon_\beta</math> is a normal function.
* The [[Von Neumann cardinal assignment|initial ordinal]] of any [[uncountable set|uncountable]] [[cardinal number|cardinal]] is an epsilon number. <math display="block">\alpha \ge 1 \Rightarrow \varepsilon_{\omega_{\alpha}} = \omega_{\alpha} \,.</math>

== Representation of ε<sub>0</sub> by rooted trees ==

Any epsilon number ε has [[Cantor normal form]] <math>\varepsilon =\omega ^{\varepsilon }</math>, which means that the Cantor normal form is not very useful for epsilon numbers. The ordinals less than {{math|''ε''<sub>0</sub>}}, however, can be usefully described by their Cantor normal forms, which leads to a representation of {{math|''ε''<sub>0</sub>}} as the ordered set of all [[Tree (graph theory)#Rooted tree|finite rooted trees]], as follows.  Any ordinal <math>\alpha<\varepsilon_0</math> has Cantor normal form <math>\alpha=\omega^{\beta_1}+\omega^{\beta_2}+\cdots+\omega^{\beta_k}</math> where ''k'' is a [[natural number]] and <math>\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_k</math>  are ordinals with <math>\alpha>\beta_1\geq\cdots\geq\beta_k</math>, uniquely determined by <math>\alpha</math>. Each of the ordinals <math>\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_k</math> in turn has a similar Cantor normal form. We obtain the finite rooted tree representing α by joining the roots of the trees representing <math>\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_k</math> to a new root. (This has the consequence that the number 0 is represented by a single root while the number <math>1=\omega^0</math> is represented by a tree containing a root and a single leaf.) An order on the set of finite rooted trees is defined recursively: we first order the subtrees joined to the root in decreasing order, and then use [[Lexicographical order|lexicographic order]] on these ordered sequences of subtrees. In this way the set of all finite rooted trees becomes a [[Well-order|well-ordered set]] which is [[order isomorphism|order isomorphic]] to {{math|''ε''<sub>0</sub>}}.

This representation is related to the proof of the [[Goodstein's theorem|hydra theorem]], which represents decreasing sequences of ordinals as a [[graph theory|graph-theoretic]] game.

==Veblen hierarchy==
{{Main|Veblen function}}
The fixed points of the "epsilon mapping" <math>x \mapsto \varepsilon_x</math> form a normal function, whose fixed points form a normal function; this is known as the [[Veblen function|Veblen hierarchy]] (the Veblen functions with base {{math|1=''φ''<sub>0</sub>(''α'') = ''ω''<sup>''α''</sup>}}).  In the notation of the Veblen hierarchy, the epsilon mapping is {{math|''φ''<sub>1</sub>}}, and its fixed points are enumerated by {{math|''φ''<sub>2</sub>}} (see [[ordinal collapsing function]].)

Continuing in this vein, one can define maps {{math|''φ''<sub>''α''</sub>}} for progressively larger ordinals α (including, by this rarefied form of transfinite recursion, limit ordinals), with progressively larger least fixed points {{math|''φ''<sub>''α''+1</sub>(0)}}.  The least ordinal not reachable from 0 by this procedure—i. e., the least ordinal α for which {{math|1=''φ''<sub>''α''</sub>(0) = ''α''}}, or equivalently the first fixed point of the map <math>\alpha \mapsto \varphi_\alpha(0)</math>—is the [[Feferman–Schütte ordinal]] {{math|Γ<sub>0</sub>}}.  In a set theory where such an ordinal can be proved to exist, one has a map {{math|Γ}} that enumerates the fixed points {{math|Γ<sub>0</sub>}}, {{math|Γ<sub>1</sub>}}, {{math|Γ<sub>2</sub>}}, ... of <math>\alpha \mapsto \varphi_\alpha(0)</math>; these are all still epsilon numbers, as they lie in the image of {{math|''φ''<sub>''β''</sub>}} for every {{math|''β'' ≤ Γ<sub>0</sub>}}, including of the map {{math|''φ''<sub>1</sub>}} that enumerates epsilon numbers.

== Surreal ε numbers ==

In ''[[On Numbers and Games]]'', the classic exposition on [[surreal number]]s, [[John Horton Conway]] provided a number of examples of concepts that had natural extensions from the ordinals to the surreals.  One such function is the [[surreal number#Powers of ω|<math>\omega</math>-map]] <math>n \mapsto \omega^n</math>; this mapping generalises naturally to include all surreal numbers in its [[domain of a function|domain]], which in turn provides a natural generalisation of the [[ordinal arithmetic#Cantor normal form|Cantor normal form]] for surreal numbers.<ref>{{cite book |author=J. H. Conway |title=[[On Numbers and Games]] |year=1976 |publisher=Academic Press |ISBN=0-12-186350-6}}</ref>

It is natural to consider any fixed point of this expanded map to be an epsilon number, whether or not it happens to be strictly an ordinal number.  Some examples of non-ordinal epsilon numbers are

:<math>\varepsilon_{-1} = \left\{0, 1, \omega, \omega^\omega, \ldots \mid \varepsilon_0 - 1, \omega^{\varepsilon_0 - 1}, \ldots\right\}</math>

and

:<math>\varepsilon_{1/2} = \left\{\varepsilon_0 + 1, \omega^{\varepsilon_0 + 1}, \ldots \mid \varepsilon_1 - 1, \omega^{\varepsilon_1 - 1}, \ldots\right\}.</math>

There is a natural way to define <math>\varepsilon_n</math> for every surreal number ''n'', and the map remains [[order-preserving]].  Conway goes on to define a broader class of "irreducible" surreal numbers that includes the epsilon numbers as a particularly interesting subclass.
